result: The authors developed FIM-ID, a novel fluorescence microscopy method for visualizing myofibrils with high resolution and contrast using standard laboratory equipment. The method utilizes SERCA immunostaining, fixation with paraformaldehyde, cryoprotection with sucrose, and image deconvolution to enable automated measurements of myofibril size and number through open-source CellProfiler pipelines.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the FIM-ID method development. Reviewer 1 called it 'a strength of the study' and noted it requires 'relatively readily available microscopy equipment.' Reviewer 2 described it as 'a useful and tractable IHC imaging method for the muscle biology field.' Reviewer 3 highlighted the 'innovative microscopy methods that should be widely available for use in other muscle biology labs.' The editor affirmed the method 'will be highly valued by the scientific community.'

result: Through optimization experiments, the authors determined that muscles fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and cryoprotected with 45% sucrose at sectioning temperatures of -30°C produced SERCA-immunoreactive cross-sections with optimal myofibril integrity and minimal freezing artifacts. Application of deconvolution algorithms dramatically increased resolution and contrast of widefield images.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed the sample preparation methodology. Reviewer 1 noted 'the development of a methodology to optimally prepare muscle samples for high-resolution imaging' as a strength. Reviewer 2 praised 'extensive validation against electron microscopy' and called the methods 'useful.' No reviewer questioned the optimization process or the resulting image quality improvements shown in the figures.

result: The automated FIM-ID measurements of myofibril CSA and myofibril number were extensively validated against manual measurements and electron microscopy. Statistical analyses showed very high agreement (R=0.9589, p=0.0002) between automated and manual measurements, with no significant differences in myofibril CSA to fiber CSA ratios or myofibril number per fiber CSA when comparing FIM-ID to EM across fiber types.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the validation. Reviewer 1 stated 'solid validation of both sample preparation and analysis' as a strength. Reviewer 2 emphasized 'extensive validation against electron microscopy' and called it 'supported by extensive validation.' Reviewer 3 noted the 'rigorous study design.' The editor confirmed 'solid validation of both sample preparation and analysis.' No concerns were raised about the validation approach or statistical comparisons.

result: Using the validated FIM-ID method, the authors discovered that mechanical overload (MOV) in mice induced significant fiber hypertrophy (28% increase overall, 39% in oxidative fibers, 25% in glycolytic fibers) that was primarily driven by myofibrillogenesis (20-22% increase in myofibril number) rather than myofibril hypertrophy (9% increase overall, inconsistent across fiber types). Myofibril number showed significant positive correlation with fiber growth magnitude, while myofibril CSA did not.
evaluation: All reviewers and the editor explicitly endorsed this finding as a major discovery. The editor stated the methods 'have been used to make the fundamental discovery of myofibrillogenesis as the mechanism of mechanical loading-induced growth.' Reviewer 1 summarized the work as reporting 'muscle cell hypertrophy...occurs primarily through an increase in the number of myofibrils (myofibrillogenesis) and not myofibril hypertrophy.' Reviewer 3 called these 'novel findings that will be beneficial to the muscle biology field.' No reviewer questioned the MOV data or conclusions.

result: In humans undergoing 7 weeks of progressive resistance exercise (RE), the authors found that SERCA1-positive (Type II) fibers showed 18% hypertrophy driven primarily by myofibrillogenesis (12% increase in myofibril number, p=0.009), with only a non-significant trend for myofibril hypertrophy. SERCA2-positive (Type I) fibers showed no significant changes. This paralleled the mouse MOV findings.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly valued the human data as confirming the mouse findings. Reviewer 1 noted the study used 'mice and humans' and that findings occur 'primarily through an increase in the number of myofibrils.' Reviewer 2 highlighted 'the usage of murine and human samples' as a strength and noted the human data provided 'detailed insight into muscle fiber hypertrophy.' Reviewer 3 praised 'different approaches to test the hypothesis.' The editor noted the discovery was made 'in mice and humans.' One reviewer noted the mouse data used young animals, but this concern was 'partly curtailed by the adult human data.'

result: Through literature review, the authors established that the longstanding myofibril splitting model has not been rigorously tested, and no previous study has demonstrated that mechanical loading increases myofibril number per fiber.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this historical context without challenge. Reviewer 2 praised 'a nice historical perspective on myofibrillogenesis in skeletal muscle' as a strength. Reviewer 3 noted the manuscript provides 'well-written and clear description of hypothesis, background, and experiments.' The gap in knowledge was implicitly accepted by all reviewers who recognized the novelty of the myofibrillogenesis findings.

result: The authors calculated that manual EM-based measurements would require tracing >180 myofibrils per fiber (>50,000 total for a two-group comparison with 7 samples per group), requiring approximately 400 hours of manual work, demonstrating the impracticality of traditional approaches.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted this rationale by praising the automated approach. Reviewer 1 noted the 'development and validation of an automated image analysis pipeline' as a strength. The time-efficiency argument was not questioned, and reviewers recognized the practical advantages of the FIM-ID method over traditional EM approaches.

result: The authors identified two distinct SERCA1-positive fiber types in mouse plantaris muscle: glycolytic (Gly) fibers that were large with few mitochondria, and oxidative (Ox) fibers that were small and enriched with intermyofibrillar mitochondria.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the fiber type classification without objection. The fiber type-specific analyses in both mouse and human studies were discussed positively by reviewers, with no concerns raised about the classification methodology or the distinction between oxidative and glycolytic SERCA1-positive fibers.

result: The authors acknowledge that the mechanisms by which mechanical loading induces myofibrillogenesis remain unknown, but note that FIM-ID now enables time- and cost-effective studies to test competing models (myofibril splitting vs. de novo myofibrillogenesis).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly noted as a weakness that 'only one time-point was assessed during hypertrophy' which 'precluded an assessment of the myofibril splitting mechanism.' This indicates the current study cannot distinguish between mechanisms, though reviewers accepted this as a limitation rather than a flaw. The editor noted that whether the mechanism applies 'in other settings of muscle growth...will require future experiments,' acknowledging the mechanistic question remains open.
